subject: physics
examHall: State the sign convention (optics, capacitors, induced EMF) before the first equation — the examiner checks consistency, not memorised signs.
Draw the circuit/diagram first, label currents and fields with directions, then write equations — solving from an unlabelled picture invites sign chaos.
Keep vector quantities (E, B, F, torque) as vectors until the final magnitude; report direction as well as size.
In derivations, name each physical law as you use it (Gauss's law, Faraday's law, de Broglie relation) — the marking scheme credits the named principle.
Check the final answer against limits: does it behave correctly as r→∞, θ→0, ω→0? A two-second sanity check catches sign and factor slips.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping the sign of a charge in Coulomb's law and then reporting a negative force magnitude, or adding field magnitudes without vector directions.
mistakes.why: Force magnitude is |q₁q₂|/4πε₀r² with direction from the geometry; a mishandled sign gives a physically impossible answer (attraction where repulsion is meant) and loses the vector marks.
mistakes.fix: Compute the magnitude from absolute charges, then decide attraction/repulsion and field direction from the charge signs on a diagram before combining fields as vectors.

mistakes.wrong: Adding capacitances in series like resistances in parallel (C = C₁ + C₂ for series), or forgetting that series capacitors carry the SAME charge.
mistakes.why: The series rule is 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ and the shared charge is the key to the voltage split; using the wrong rule cascades into wrong energies and loses the whole calculation.
mistakes.fix: Write the two rules side by side on scratch (parallel: same V, C adds; series: same Q, reciprocal C), then decide which applies from the circuit before substituting.

mistakes.wrong: Changing sign conventions mid-loop, or treating a junction equation as a loop equation.
mistakes.why: Kirchhoff's rules are sign-bookkeeping; one inconsistent sign makes two loop equations contradictory and the whole 4-5 mark network question collapses.
mistakes.fix: Choose directions for all currents on the diagram, write the junction rule (ΣI in = ΣI out) separately from loops, and traverse every loop in one fixed direction applying ΣV = 0 with the same sign rules.

mistakes.wrong: Confusing which resistance goes in the left gap, or reading the null point without interchanging gaps to check.
mistakes.why: The balance condition S = R·l/(100−l) presumes the standard setup; the interchange check is what proves there is no end error — skipping it loses the experimental-mark band.
mistakes.fix: Redraw the bridge, name the gaps, apply the balance relation with the correct l, and mention the interchange-of-gaps check (and end error) in the error-analysis part.

mistakes.wrong: Using the right-hand rule where the left-hand rule applies (or vice versa), or reversing the induced current direction in Lenz's law.
mistakes.why: F = BIL (force on a current) uses the LEFT hand; the dynamo rule for induced EMF uses the RIGHT hand. Swapping them reverses the direction answer — and Lenz's-law questions award the direction explicitly.
mistakes.fix: Write the mnemonic on the margin: motor = left (Force), dynamo/generator = right (EMF). For Lenz's law, ask 'which induced current opposes the change?' and verify the flux change first.

mistakes.wrong: Using flux = BA when the field is at an angle θ to the normal without cosθ, or differentiating B instead of Φ.
mistakes.why: Φ = BA cosθ and EMF = −dΦ/dt; missing cosθ or differentiating the wrong quantity gives an EMF that is wrong by a factor or by zero (when B is constant but area changes).
mistakes.fix: Define the angle θ between B and the NORMAL to the coil, write Φ = BA cosθ explicitly, then differentiate whichever quantity (B, A or θ) actually changes.

mistakes.wrong: Using peak values in power formulas (P = V₀I₀ instead of V_rms I_rms), or confusing rms with average for a full sine cycle.
mistakes.why: Average power uses rms values (V₀/√2, I₀/√2); the average of a sine over a full cycle is ZERO, not its rms. Mixing them doubles the power or zeroes it — both are marked wrong.
mistakes.fix: Label every voltage/current as peak or rms on the diagram, convert once at the start (V_rms = V₀/√2), and remember ⟨sin²⟩ = ½ is why rms exists.

mistakes.wrong: Using the lens formula with the mirror sign convention, or assigning f positive for a concave (diverging) lens.
mistakes.why: The Cartesian convention makes a diverging lens f negative and a concave mirror f negative; mixing conventions produces a virtual/real flip and the magnification sign follows wrongly.
mistakes.fix: At the top of the solution write the convention, then derive signs from the ray diagram: incident light left→right, distances against light negative. Check the answer against the diagram's image position.

mistakes.wrong: Dropping the λ/2 half-wave shift at a reflection, or using the small-angle approximation outside its valid range.
mistakes.why: Fringe positions depend on the exact path difference (nλ vs (n+½)λ); a missing phase flip swaps bright and dark fringes and loses the whole interference analysis.
mistakes.fix: Write the path difference with its phase condition (bright: nλ; dark: (n+½)λ) and note any reflection phase flip before computing fringe spacing β = λD/d.

mistakes.wrong: Assuming brighter light always ejects more energetic electrons, or using work function in J while photon energy is in eV.
mistakes.why: Intensity changes the NUMBER of photoelectrons; frequency sets their maximum KE (hν − φ). Mixing eV and joules shifts every answer by 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ — a systematic mark loss.
mistakes.fix: Separate the two knobs (frequency → energy, intensity → count), write Einstein's equation KE_max = hν − φ, and convert units once, explicitly (1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J).

mistakes.wrong: Quoting rₙ ∝ n (instead of n²) or Eₙ ∝ 1/n (instead of 1/n²), or forgetting the Z² factor for hydrogen-like ions.
mistakes.why: The scaling laws rₙ ∝ n²/Z, Eₙ ∝ −Z²/n² are the whole derivation; a wrong power or missing Z loses the series of marks built on it, including the spectral-line calculation.
mistakes.fix: Memorise the pair as 'radius grows as n², energy climbs toward zero as 1/n², both scale with Z²', and check the sign: bound-state energies are negative.

mistakes.wrong: Balancing a decay equation for mass number but not charge, or applying half-life linearly instead of exponentially.
mistakes.why: Both conservation laws must hold (A and Z); and after n half-lives the remainder is N₀/2ⁿ, not N₀(1 − n/2). The linear habit gives absurd answers (negative atoms) that examiners penalise fully.
mistakes.fix: Write the decay equation with A and Z conserved, and compute activity/remaining nuclei with N = N₀(½)^(t/T½) or N = N₀e^(−λt) — checking A and Z at the end.

questions.question: Two capacitors in series carry different charges — true or false, and why does the answer decide the whole calculation?
questions.solution: False. In series the SAME charge sits on every capacitor (charge conservation on the intermediate plates); the VOLTAGES differ, V = Q/C each. That is why the series rule is 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂. In parallel the voltages are equal and the charges differ. Deciding 'same Q or same V' first is the fastest guard against using the wrong combination rule — the error cascades into every energy and voltage answer.

questions.question: Why does the induced current in a coil reverse when you reverse the direction you push a magnet in — and which hand do you use?
questions.solution: Lenz's law: the induced current opposes the CHANGE in flux. Pushing the magnet's north pole in creates increasing flux inward, so the coil's near face becomes north to repel it; pulling it out reverses the change, so the current reverses. For the direction of induced EMF/current use the RIGHT hand (dynamo rule); the LEFT hand is for the force on a current-carrying wire (motor rule). Swapping the hands is the classic direction error.

questions.question: A heater rated '240 V, 1000 W' runs on 240 V rms. What power does a student get who plugs in the peak voltage by mistake?
questions.solution: Peak = 240√2 ≈ 339 V. Using P = V²/R with the peak gives 2000 W — exactly double, because P_rms = V_rms²/R = (V₀²/2)/R. Average power always uses rms values; the rms exists precisely because ⟨sin²ωt⟩ = ½. Label every AC quantity as peak or rms before substituting, and convert once at the start.

questions.question: In Young's double-slit experiment, why do bright and dark fringes swap if one beam reflects off a denser medium on the way?
questions.solution: Reflection off a denser medium adds a π phase flip — an extra λ/2 path difference. The condition for brightness becomes (n+½)λ instead of nλ, so every bright fringe becomes dark and vice versa. Always write the path difference AND its phase condition before computing fringe positions; a missing half-wave shift is an invisible sign error that the diagram will not catch.

questions.question: Does a brighter torch eject faster photoelectrons than a dim ultraviolet lamp? Set the examiner straight with the two equations.
questions.solution: No. Frequency sets the maximum kinetic energy: KE_max = hν − φ (Einstein's photoelectric equation). Intensity sets only the NUMBER of electrons per second (photon count). A dim UV source with hν > φ ejects fewer but faster electrons than a bright red source below threshold, which ejects none. Also convert units once: work functions are quoted in eV, hν in J — 1 eV = 1.6×10⁻¹⁹ J.

questions.question: After 3 half-lives, is one-and-a-half of the original nuclei left? Show the correct bookkeeping.
questions.solution: No — remaining fraction = (½)³ = 1/8, not 1 − 3/2. Decay is exponential: N = N₀(½)^(t/T½) = N₀e^(−λt) with λ = ln2/T½. The linear habit gives negative atom counts for t > 2T½, which is physically absurd and loses the whole question. Also balance decay equations on BOTH mass number A and atomic number Z.

questions.question: Why do Kirchhoff loop equations sometimes come out contradictory, and how do you prevent it?
questions.solution: Because the sign convention changed mid-solution. Fix the current directions on the diagram first, then traverse every loop in ONE fixed direction: battery EMF positive when traversed − to +, IR negative when traversed along the current. Write the junction rule separately (ΣI in = ΣI out). If two loop equations then contradict, the diagram's current directions were wrong — flip one and re-solve rather than patching signs ad hoc.

questions.question: A convex lens question asks for the image. Why does the examiner care which convention you announce?
questions.solution: Because the same formula 1/f = 1/v − 1/u gives different v for different sign assignments, and only the announced convention makes the answer checkable. State the Cartesian convention (incident light left→right; distances measured against the light are negative; a diverging lens has f < 0), derive signs from the labelled ray diagram, and verify the final image position against the diagram. Consistency — not memorised signs — is what the marks reward.
